1.pericope_label: If it had not been the Lord who was on our side: the swallowing pit and the proud waters

schools.summary: Augustine reads the title as an ascent made by the affections rather than the feet, and explains the shifting between one singer and many by the unity of the body, adding that the martyrs have already sung the song.

Calvin defends the ascription to David and dismisses both the deportation setting and the prophetic evasion as unfounded, yet refuses to limit the psalm to one occasion; Gill reads the swallowing through the earth that took Korah, the fish that took Jonah, and the beasts of prey.

Henry marvels that the danger came from men rather than beasts and observes that God lets enemies prevail far so that the deliverance may be the more illustrious; Spurgeon judges the opening a fragment better left in its broken grandeur than patched with italics.

Clarke shows the title missing from the ancient versions, dates the psalm long after David and ties it to the plot of Haman, and keeps the figure of an earthquake swallowing a city alive; Wesley reads the proud waters of a numerous and raging enemy.

Ellicott dates the psalm late from the singular word for man and from a rare form, and traces the shift of imagery from earthquake to flood; Keil and Delitzsch find the ascription textually unestablished and the Aramaizing style and verbal play indicative of a modern origin.

debates: When was the psalm written? Clarke shows the ascription to David missing from the manuscripts, the ancient versions and most of the fathers, and proposes the escape from the massacre planned by Haman; Keil and Delitzsch call the ascription textually unestablished and find a modern origin in the Aramaizing character and the taste for verbal play; Ellicott argues from the singular term for man, which implies a world already divided in two, and from a rare later form; Calvin alone defends the title, rejects the deportation setting and calls the prophetic reading forced, yet declines to limit the psalm to David time.

Is the danger an earthquake or a beast of prey? Gill offers the earth that swallowed Korah, the fish that swallowed Jonah, or ravenous beasts; Ellicott makes the allusion to Korah certain from the shared verb and adjective and notes that the imagery then shifts abruptly to a flood; Clarke keeps the chasm that swallows a city alive; Henry prefers a lamb devoured by a lion.
outliers: Spurgeon judges the opening sentence a fragment that had better have been left in its broken grandeur than patched with the italics of the received version, and supplies his own unfinished rendering of it.

Ellicott infers the date from a single general term, arguing that a writer who divides the whole world into two parts treats as an accomplished fact what the prophets had held only as an ideal of the future.
themes: a song of ascents in its risings

6.pericope_label: Blessed be the Lord: the prey delivered from the teeth, the bird from the snare, and the help that is in his name

schools.summary: Henry infers that the enemies had no power except what was given from above and puts the whole rescue in the breaking of the snare, and reads the plural of the last verse as the concern of the public; Spurgeon adds that the more imminent the danger the more eminent the mercy, itemises the fowler methods, and turns the making of heaven and earth into a double assurance.
Gill presses the likeness of the bird in its weakness, fear and worthlessness, makes the fowlers Satan and his agents, and draws from the close that help is in the Lord only and in no creature.

Clarke reads the psalm off one historical deliverance, with the snare broken by an improbable providence and the poacher caught in his own trap, guesses at its author, and takes the closing name of the Chaldee version as the substantial Word.

Keil and Delitzsch make the two figures deliberate, beasts for bloodthirstiness and fowlers for cunning, and correct the construction of the bird clause from the accents; Ellicott treats the change of figure as one more rapid transition.

debates: Why do the figures change from teeth to snare within two verses? Keil and Delitzsch make the pairing deliberate, beasts of prey standing for bloodthirstiness as the world empires do in the book of Daniel and fowlers for cunning; Clarke values the second image because it shows the weakness of the people and the craft of their enemies at once; Spurgeon marks the movement away from the flood; Ellicott sees only another rapid transition to a favourite figure.

What does the closing appeal to the name amount to? Clarke follows the Chaldee in reading the name of the Word of the Lord and takes it of the substantial Word rather than of anything spoken; Gill draws that help is in the Lord only and in no creature; Henry argues that the God of Israel is the maker of the world and will therefore have a church in it; Spurgeon takes the making of heaven and earth as two distinct pledges.
outliers: Clarke identifies the psalm with a single deliverance so confidently that he names the book which tells that story as probably the best comment on the psalm, and guesses that its hero was the author.

Keil and Delitzsch correct the received construction from the accentuation, so that the text does not say the soul is like a bird that has escaped but that the soul is as a bird, the escape being stated on its own.
themes: power granted to enemies only from above
the snare broken rather than avoided
help located in the name of the maker
